"So then the senior grabbed my bag," Kiran said, "and I just stared him down."
"Last week you said you pushed him," said Madhav.
"I did push him. A bit. After staring."
"And yesterday there were three seniors."
The others laughed. Kiran's face went hot. "There were three. Two were just watching."
On the way to the bus Madhav said quietly, "Kiran, I was there. He asked for his bag strap back, you gave it, and we walked off. That's it."
"Everyone was listening," Kiran said. "If I tell it like that, it's boring."
"But you have to remember which version you told to who. Doesn't that get tiring?"
Kiran didn't answer, just kicked a stone all the way to the bus stop.

qa.q: What did Madhav say really happened with the senior?
qa.a: Madhav said the senior asked for his bag strap back, Kiran gave it, and they walked off.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel when the others laughed, and why does the story keep growing?
qa.a: Kiran felt embarrassed, face going hot, and keeps making the story bigger out of worry that the plain version would seem boring to everyone listening.

qa.q: What could Kiran try the next time the group asks about the fight?
qa.a: Kiran could tell the plain version with a joke, trusting that people like Madhav value an honest story over a dramatic one.

qa.q: What is it like for Madhav to hear the story change each time?
qa.a: Madhav, who was there, finds it awkward and tiring, and cares enough to point out the cost privately rather than in front of everyone.

grounding: A teenager's story of a small clash with a senior grows each retelling to keep status, and a peer points out the strain of remembering every version.

passage:
I'm Rajni, and in Class 10 I became someone who couldn't just say a number. In the prelims I got 78 in maths. When Pooja's group asked, I said 88. By lunch it had become 90, "but the teacher cut marks unfairly". On the group call that night, it was 92.
The worst part wasn't the lie. It was the remembering. I had to keep track of which person had heard which version, and once I caught myself saying 88 to someone who had heard 92. My stomach dropped.
When the real mark sheets were put up, Pooja saw mine. She didn't say anything cruel. She just said, "You didn't need to." Looking back, the 78 would have been fine. It was the 92 I couldn't carry.

qa.q: What mark did Rajni actually get in maths in the prelims?
qa.a: Rajni got 78 in maths in the prelims.

qa.q: What does Rajni's stomach dropping suggest?
qa.a: It suggests fear of being caught, because keeping track of different versions for different people had become stressful.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Rajni have done differently?
qa.a: Each retelling pushed the number higher until it couldn't be kept straight; saying 78 honestly at the start would have been far easier to carry.

qa.q: How might Pooja have felt when she saw the real mark sheet?
qa.a: Pooja seemed more sad than angry; her words "You didn't need to" suggest she would have accepted the real mark.

grounding: A teenager inflates a maths mark to impress peers, and the number grows with every retelling until remembering the versions becomes a burden.
